notes: Cameron and Trivedi (2005), section 23.3, pp. 792-5, Table 23.1, program mma23p1pannonlin.do (read, cameron.econ.ucdavis.edu/mmabook): on the 346 firms in 1975-79 (drop if year<75) it fits xtpoisson PAT LOGR, re i(id) (the Poisson-RE column, Stata's default gamma firm effects) and xtpoisson PAT LOGR, re i(id) normal (normal firm effects), beside pooled Poisson, Poisson-FE and GEE; its id = _n is the firm, here obsno. RULE GAP: the table's column names are shifted against the help page's: the column named logr holds the current patent count PAT (integers; for firm 1 the 1972-79 counts in logr3, logr2, logr1 and logr sum to its sumpat), logr1-logr4 hold the patents lagged 1-4 years, logr5 holds the current log R&D LOGR (negative for firm 2) and pat-pat4 hold log R&D lagged 1-5 years; the formula names the columns as the table names them. Ignored: cusip (Compustat firm number, an alias of obsno), sumpat (patents 1972-79, includes the response) and the lagged patent counts logr1-logr4. year codes 1975-79 as 1-5, and the book's model has no year terms. Hall, Griliches and Hausman (1986) fit the same panel with distributed lags of log R&D.

formula: log(gsp) ~ log(pcap) + log(pc) + log(emp) + unemp + (1 | state)
notes: plm's vignette B_plmFunction.Rmd (read, cran/plm) fits Baltagi's error-components model on plm's copy of this table (plm adds region): PrSwar <- plm(log(gsp) ~ log(pcap) + log(pc) + log(emp) + unemp, Produc, model = "random", random.method = "swar", random.dfcor = 3), random state intercepts by Swamy-Arora. The help page cites Baltagi and Pinnoi (1995), titled Public capital stock and state productivity growth: further evidence from an error components model (48 states, 1970-86, state-specific effects; abstract on IDEAS/RePEc), and Baltagi's Econometric Analysis of Panel Data. hwy, water and util are the components of public capital pc, used only in plm's nested state-within-region model, whose region column this table lacks; ignored. year is not in this model.

formula: log(gsp) ~ log(pcap) + log(pc) + log(emp) + unemp + (1 | state) + (1 | year)
notes: plm's vignette B_plmFunction.Rmd (read, cran/plm): Baltagi (2009) pp. 60-62 presents EViews' two-way random-effects output for Produc, reproduced as Prw <- plm(log(gsp) ~ log(pcap) + log(pc) + log(emp) + unemp, Produc, model = "random", random.method = "walhus", effect = "twoways", random.dfcor = 3) and its Swamy-Arora update: crossed state and year intercepts. The vignette notes that the estimated year variance is negative under Wallace-Hussain and Swamy-Arora and set to 0. hwy, water and util ignored as in row 1.

Penn World Table 5 panel of 125 countries, 1960-85, one row per country and year (help page). The help page cites Hayashi (2000), Econometrics, chapter 5 (Panel Data), pp. 358-363, recalled, not read: the chapter's growth application estimates a Solow model with country effects after Islam (1995) on five-year intervals, its regressors (lagged log income, the log saving rate, population growth) derived from these columns. Hayashi's data page could not be fetched, so whether a random-effects fit is reported stays unconfirmed and published_model is no. Formula proposed on the annual table: log real GDP per capita on the saving rate (in percent, which can be negative, so not logged) and log population with year effects and a country random intercept. opec and com mark country groups (Islam's sample restrictions), left out of the formula.

formula: tmathssk ~ classk + totexpk + sex + freelunk + race + (1 | schidkn)
notes: Project STAR kindergarten, students in schools (schidkn, the school indicator). The help page cites Stock and Watson (2003), Introduction to Econometrics, chapter 11 (experiments and quasi-experiments), recalled, not read: the kindergarten differences estimates regress the student's total of the math and reading scaled scores on the class-type indicators (classk: small class, regular with aide), adding teacher experience (totexpk), school indicator variables, and sex, free-lunch eligibility and race. Schools enter as fixed effects, so the school is rendered as a random intercept and published_model is no. RULE GAP: the book's response is the sum tmathssk + treadssk, which is no column; the two scores are filed as two rows, each ignoring the other.

formula: treadssk ~ classk + totexpk + sex + freelunk + race + (1 | schidkn)
notes: As row 1 with the reading scaled score; tmathssk ignored. Stock and Watson (2003) chapter 11, recalled: the response there is the total of both scores, with school indicators as fixed effects.

formula: I(choice == "choice1") ~ 0 + I(price1 - price2) + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) + (0 + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) | id)
notes: mlogit's vignette c5.mxl.qmd (read, cran/mlogit) fits mixed logits on mlogit's copy of this table (the same 2929 stated-preference choices of Meijer and Rouwendal, the attributes named price_A to comfort_B there): Train.mxlu <- mlogit(choice ~ price + time + change + comfort | - 1, Tr, panel = TRUE, rpar = c(time = "n", change = "n", comfort = "n"), R = 100, correlation = FALSE, halton = NA, method = "bhhh"), then Train.mxlc <- update(Train.mxlu, correlation = TRUE): correlated normal coefficients on time, change and comfort per individual (id), a fixed price coefficient and no alternative intercept (price rescaled to euros and time to hours there). With two alternatives the conditional logit is a logit of choosing choice1 on the attribute differences, so the formula renders the correlated model on I(x1 - x2). Meijer and Rouwendal (2006), cited by the help page, fit random-coefficient logits to these data. RULE GAP: the differences are no columns, so covariates list the eight attribute columns and random_slopes stays blank. choiceid numbers an individual's choice tasks, ignored.

formula: Tuna.choice ~ brand intercepts + price.<brand> (conditional logit, one price coefficient across the five brands) + household random brand intercepts and price slope by Tuna.hid
notes: Kim, Blattberg and Rossi (1995), JBES 13(3), 291-303, cited by the help page, abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc: a random-coefficient logit in which brand-specific intercepts and price-slope coefficients vary across households, fitted to household panel data of two product categories, its parametric heterogeneity distribution checked against semiparametric density estimates. Tuna.hid the household, Tuna.id its purchase occasions (ignored), Tuna.choice the brand chosen among five (Starkist and Chicken of the Sea in water and oil, store label in water), price.<brand> each brand's price at the purchase. RULE GAP: a multinomial (conditional) logit is outside Family, so family is blank, and the price slope sits on the alternatives' prices, which no one column holds. The paper's full specification was not read, hence medium.

formula: lnexp12m ~ lntotal + age + sex + hhsize + farm + educyr + (1 | commune)
notes: The help page cites Cameron and Trivedi (2005) pp. 88-90, the quantile regression of lnmed on lntotal in mma04p2qreg.do (qreg0902.dta: sex, age, educyr98, farm, urban98, hhsize, lhhexp1, lhhex12m, lnrlfood), with no commune term. The same book's section 24.7, pp. 848-53, Table 24.4, program mma24p1olscluster.do (read), takes the 5999 households of vietnam_ex1.dta in 194 communes and fits xtreg LNEXP12M LNHHEXP AGE SEX HHSIZE FARM EDUC, re and , mle after iis COMMUNE (random commune intercepts), beside OLS with cluster-robust errors and commune fixed effects. LNEXP12M is lnexp12m (lhhex12m) and LNHHEXP lntotal (lhhexp1); EDUC there is comped98 (completed diploma), which this table lacks, so educyr (years of schooling) stands in, hence medium. lnmed repeats lhhex12m under the quantile regression's name, ignored; urban and lnrlfood are not in the model.

formula: pharvis ~ lnhhexp + insurance + sex + age + married + illdays + actdays + injury + illness + educ + (1 | commune)
notes: Cameron and Trivedi (2005), section 24.7, pp. 848-53, Table 24.6, cited by the help page, program mma24p2poiscluster.do (read): vietnam_ex2.dta holds these individuals and columns (COMPED98 = educ, ILLDUM = illness, INJDUM = injury, HLTHINS = insurance, lnhhinc = lnhhexp) in 194 communes; it fits poisson PHARVIS with cluster-robust errors and, after iis COMMUNE, xtpois PHARVIS LNHHEXP INSURANCE SEX AGE MARRIED ILLDAYS ACTDAYS INJURY ILLNESS EDUC, re (Table 24.6 columns 5-6; Stata's default gamma commune effects, rendered as (1 | commune)) beside the fixed-effects Poisson. age holds the log of age, as the program's summary shows; lnhhexp is log household total expenditure in the program, though the help page calls it total medical expenditure.

formula: choice ~ brand intercepts + feat.<brand> + price.<brand> (conditional logit, one feature and one price coefficient across the four brands) + household random coefficients on the brand intercepts, feature and price by id (discrete support points)
notes: Jain, Vilcassim and Chintagunta (1994), JBES 12(3), 317-28, cited by the help page, abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc: A Random-Coefficients Logit Brand-Choice Model Applied to Panel Data, households differing in brand preferences and in their responses to marketing variables, the unknown heterogeneity distribution approximated by a discrete distribution. id the household making repeated purchases, choice the brand bought among four, feat.<brand> and price.<brand> each brand's newspaper feature and price. RULE GAP: a multinomial (conditional) logit is outside Family, so family is blank; the random coefficients have discrete support points rather than a normal distribution, rendered as household random effects. The same purchases in long form are rabe_hesketh yogurt.dta, where Rabe-Hesketh and Skrondal fit a mixed logit with correlated household brand effects.
